The passage discusses two different topics: command hallucinations and olfactory hallucinations (phantosmia and parosmia).

Command hallucinations are voices that people hear and are told what to do. These can range from simple commands like "Stand up" or "Shut the door" to more threatening commands. Compliance with these hallucinations can vary, but they are often associated with schizophrenia. Some questions that can help determine if someone may be experiencing command hallucinations include: "What are the voices telling you to do?", "When did your voices first start telling you to do things?", "Do you recognize the person who is telling you to harm yourself (or others)?", "Do you think you can resist doing what the voices are telling you to do?"

Olfactory hallucinations, on the other hand, are smelling an odor that is not actually there. Parosmia is a related condition where a real odor is perceived as a different scent than remembered. These distortions to the sense of smell can be caused by a range of conditions such as nasal infections, nasal polyps, dental problems, migraines, head injuries, seizures, strokes, or brain tumors. Environmental exposures can also cause it, such as smoking or certain chemicals.

The last part of the passage seems unrelated to the previous topics and appears to be a fictional character description from a novel. The character is a deaf man who fought in the Spanish war and is a Communist. The passage does not provide any context or connection to the previous topics.
